summary: The covenant laws forbid corrupt testimony and oppression, require help even for an enemy's animal, and establish rest for land, workers, foreigners, and livestock alongside three annual festivals. The closing promises describe divine guidance and well-being in the land, but also the gradual expulsion of its inhabitants and the destruction of their worship.
whyItMatters: Justice is worked out through courts, ordinary help, and rhythms that protect those with little power. The same covenant speech then envisions a homeland through exclusion and displacement, a distinct and difficult part of its promise.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: The end of the covenant ordinances at Sinai, looking ahead to farming, worship, and settlement in the land.
context.literaryForm: Social and judicial commands, agricultural and festival calendar, and a conditional promise of guidance and conquest.

before.text: The laws have forbidden oppression of foreigners, widows, orphans, and poor borrowers. This chapter develops those obligations through courts, work, rest, and dealings with enemies.

here.text: The first part orders communal life; the final part turns toward a guided journey and a land whose present inhabitants will be driven out.

after.text: Moses reports the words to the people, writes them, and presides over a covenant ceremony with sacrifices, blood, and the people's pledged obedience.

outline.heading: Truthful justice and help for enemies
outline.note: Crowds, wealth, poverty, and hostility must not corrupt testimony or excuse neglect.

outline.heading: Rest for land and living beings
outline.note: Seventh-year fallow and seventh-day rest include the poor, animals, servants, and foreigners.

outline.heading: Three festivals and offering rules
outline.note: Unleavened bread, harvest, and ingathering order the worshiping year.

outline.heading: The angel and the demand for allegiance
outline.note: Guidance is joined to obedience and rejection of the inhabitants’ worship.

outline.heading: Well-being and gradual displacement
outline.note: Promises of health and increase accompany the progressive removal of other peoples.

outline.heading: Boundaries and exclusion
outline.note: The speech specifies borders and forbids covenants and continued residence that might lead to other worship.

keyVerses.text: If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him. You shall surely help him with it.
keyVerses.why: An enemy’s hostility does not remove the obligation to help his burdened animal.

keyVerses.text: “Six days you shall do your work, and on the seventh day you shall rest, that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant, and the alien may be refreshed.
keyVerses.why: Weekly rest expressly includes livestock, a servant’s son, and the foreigner.

keyVerses.text: Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and inherit the land.
keyVerses.why: The land promise is explicitly connected to the gradual expulsion of existing inhabitants.

questions.question: Do the court rules favor the rich or the poor?
questions.answer: They forbid both favoring a poor litigant simply for being poor and denying the poor justice. False reports, crowd pressure, and bribery are also rejected, so the standard is a truthful judgment rather than automatic loyalty to one social group.

questions.question: Why mention an enemy’s livestock?
questions.answer: An obligation to return a wandering animal and help a fallen burdened donkey remains even when its owner is hostile. The commands make the treatment of an enemy concrete in daily actions, without requiring that the personal conflict first be settled.

questions.question: What does leaving land “fallow” accomplish?
questions.answer: The land rests from its usual sowing and gathering in the seventh year, allowing the poor to eat and animals to take what remains. The rule therefore connects agricultural rest with access to food beyond the landholder's household.

questions.question: Who benefits from weekly rest?
questions.answer: The stated beneficiaries include the worker, ox, donkey, servant's son, and foreigner. Rest is presented as refreshment shared across unequal positions rather than a privilege only for the household head.

questions.question: What are the three annual festivals?
questions.answer: The chapter names unleavened bread in the departure month, harvest with first fruits, and ingathering at the end of the agricultural year. All the males must appear before God, and the commands join remembered rescue to the produce of the land.

questions.question: Who is the angel sent ahead?
questions.answer: God describes a messenger who will guard the way and bring the people to the prepared place, bearing divine authority because God's name is in him. The chapter gives no personal name, so identifying him with a later named figure goes beyond the description.

questions.question: Are the promises of health a universal guarantee for every reader?
questions.answer: They belong to this covenant address about serving God in the land, including bread, water, fertility, and length of life. The chapter does not authorize blaming an ill or infertile person for insufficient faith.

questions.question: Does the land promise involve displacement of other people?
questions.answer: Yes. God promises to drive out named peoples gradually and orders Israel to expel the inhabitants, destroy their worship, and make no covenant with them. The explanation combines religious loyalty with concern about population and wild animals. The speech addresses the ancient covenant community and its envisioned settlement.

glossary.def: Land left without its usual cultivation and gathering in the seventh year.
The annual festival associated here with gathering the field’s produce at the end of the year.
An image of a trap used for the danger of serving the inhabitants’ gods.
